newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - N. Ireland mother, daughter torment UK establishment.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - N. Ireland mother, daughter torment UK establishment.

text.p: In January 1972 a fiery young Catholic woman deputy from Northern Ireland created a sensation by punching Britain's interior minister in the face during an emergency debate in parliament.

Mini-skirted, petite and unleashing verbal upper-cuts that frequently floored parliamentarians, Bernadette McAliskey was the enfant terrible of a civil rights campaign that changed the face of British rule over Protestant Northern Ireland.
More than a quarter of a century later, her heavily pregnant daughter Roisin is making life just as uncomfortable for the British establishment.

Roisin, 25, is in prison awaiting extradition proceedings by the German authorities who want to question her about an Irish Republican Army (IRA) bomb attack on a British military base in Osnabruck last year. She denies involvement.

The decision to keep her in a top security wing, where she underwent 75 strip searches in four months, provoked an official complaint from Ireland and protests by human rights campaigners in the United States and Canada.
Now, in a move designed to pressure the authorities into releasing her to have the baby, she will stand in her mother's old Northern Ireland constituency in the British general election on May 1.
BOTH COMMITTED NATIONALISTS
Mother and daughter are committed nationalists who want to see the end of British rule in Northern Ireland, where more than 3,000 people have died in 25 years of conflict.

Bernadette McAliskey, known as Bernadette Devlin until her 1973 marriage, was feted on both sides of the Atlantic as an articulate opponent of what she saw as anti-Catholic bias by Northern Ireland's local Protestant rulers.

She withdrew from the political frontlines after Protestant gunmen pumped nine bullets into her in 1981 but has not lost the power to shock. "I have said I find the use of violence understandable," she told an interviewer earlier this month.
"That would go for Roisin, too. Frankly, I can think of more traumatic things than finding out my daughter is a terrorist."
The European Parliament plans to send a delegation to London's Holloway prison to investigate complaints about Roisin's treatment since her arrest last November.
Earlier this month the government eased Roisin's prison conditions but sparked more protests by refusing to release her on bail to in time to give birth. She is eight months pregnant.
To make matters worse, Home Office minister David Maclean found himself dragged into the controversy by effectively calling her "evil scum" and accusing her of being an IRA member.

"The situation could hardly be bettered for those who wish to depict the British justice system as a brutal and heartless; for government ministers it is a public relations nightmare over which they have no control," said the Daily Telegraph.
Just as difficult for ministers must be the sight of Bernadette once again campaigning actively against the government, this time on behalf of her daughter.
A rare shot of the two women together showed them carrying the coffin of an anti-British guerrilla, Catholic gunman Dominic "Mad Dog" McGlinchey, at his 1994 funeral.
Bernadette then made a graveside speech in which she described McGlinchey as "the finest republican the struggle has ever produced".
THE YOUNG BERNADETTE

The comments did not surprise those who remember the young Bernadette Devlin. She stormed into parliament aged 22 in 1969, the youngest woman elected to Britain's lower house. She lost her seat in 1974.

Northern Ireland's troubles were heating up when she came into public life. A famous 1969 picture showed her using a sledge hammer to break rocks for protesters to throw at police, which led to a six-month jail term for inciting a riot.

The most dramatic moment of her spell in parliament came in 1972 during a speech by Conservative Home Secretary Reginald Maudling after British troops had shot dead 13 unarmed Catholic demonstrators in Londonderry.

"I walked down calmly to the fancy bit in the middle and I bowed to the Speaker. Then I walked over and I caught the Home Secretary by the throat and gave him a smack in the gob (mouth)," she told an interviewer.

"At that point a Tory (Conservative) leapt up and hit me an unmerciful blow and then another MP jumped up and cuffed him, knocking him on to the lower bench. I left quickly, leaving a whole pile of MPs literally boxing on the floor of the House."
Any thoughts of retiring from the political scene vanished when Roisin was arrested.
"All I see is that nothing has changed. When a young pregnant Irish woman can still be imprisoned for four months without charge...in 25 years where have we really got to?" she said.
